source_text: Ἔστι δὲ ὁ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς αἰτίας λόγος, ἐὰν ἐπισκοπῶμεν πότερον ἁπλῶς καὶ μάτην γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος ἤ τινος ἕνεκεν· εἰ δέ τινος ἕνεκεν, πότερον ἐπὶ τοῦτο γενόμενον αὐτὸ τὸ ζῆν καὶ διαμένειν καθ᾿ ἣν ἐγένετο φύσιν ἢ διὰ χρείαν τινός· εἰ δὲ κατὰ χρείαν, ἤτοι τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν αὐτῷ προσηκόντων καὶ πλείονος φροντίδος ἠξιωμένων. Ὃ δὴ καὶ κοινότερον σκοποῦντες εὑρίσκομεν ὅτι πᾶς εὖ φρονῶν καὶ λογικῇ κρίσει πρὸς τὸ ποιεῖν τι κινούμενος οὐδὲν ὧν κατὰ πρόθεσιν ἐνεργεῖ ποιεῖ μάτην, ἀλλ᾿ ἤτοι τῆς ἰδίας ἕνεκεν χρήσεως ἢ διὰ χρείαν ἄλλου τινὸς ὧν πεφρόντικεν ἢ δι᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ γινόμενον, ὁλκῇ τινι φυσικῇ καὶ στοργῇ πρὸς τὴν αὐτοῦ γένεσιν κινούμενος· οἷον (λεγέσθω γὰρ δι᾿ εἰκόνος τινός, ἵνα σαφὲς γένηται τὸ προκείμενον) ἄνθρωπος ποιεῖ μὲν οἶκον διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν χρείαν, ποιεῖ δὲ βουσὶ καὶ καμήλοις ἢ τοῖς ἄλλοις ζώοις, ὧν ἐστιν ἐνδεής, τὴν ἑκάστῳ τούτων ἁρμόζουσαν σκέπην, οὐκ ἰδίας ἕνεκεν χρήσεως κατὰ τὸ φαινόμενον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ μὲν τὸ τέλος διὰ τοῦτο, κατὰ δὲ τὸ προσεχὲς διὰ τὴν τούτων ὧν πεφρόντικεν ἐπιμέλειαν· ποιεῖται δὲ καὶ παῖδας οὔτε διὰ χρείαν ἰδίαν οὔτε δι᾿ ἕτερόν τι τῶν αὐτῷ προσηκόντων, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ τῷ εἶναί τε καὶ διαμένειν καθ᾿ ὅσον οἷόν τε τοὺς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γεννωμένους, τῇ τῶν παίδων καὶ τῶν ἐγγόνων διαδοχῇ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τελευτὴν παραμυθούμενος καὶ ταύτῃ τὸ θνητὸν ἀπαθανατίζειν οἰόμενος. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ὑπὸ τούτων. Ὁ μέντοι θεὸς οὔτ᾿ ἂν μάτην ἐποίησε τὸν ἄνθρωπον· ἔστι γὰρ σοφός, οὐδὲν δὲ σοφίας ἔργον μάταιον· οὔτε διὰ χρείαν ἰδίαν· παντὸς γάρ ἐστιν ἀπροσδεής. Τῷ δὲ μηδενὸς δεομένῳ τὸ παράπαν οὐδὲν τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γενομένων συντελέσειεν ἂν εἰς χρείαν ἰδίαν. Ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ διά τινα τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γενομένων ἔργων ἐποίησε τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Οὐδὲν γὰρ τῶν λόγῳ καὶ κρίσει χρωμένων οὔτε τῶν μειζόνων οὔτε τῶν καταδεεστέρων γέγονεν ἢ γίνεται πρὸς ἑτέρου χρείαν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν τῶν γενομένων ζωήν τε καὶ διαμονήν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ λόγος εὑρίσκει τινὰ χρείαν τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων γενέσεως αἰτίαν, τῶν μὲν ἀθανάτων ἀνενδεῶν ὄντων καὶ μηδεμιᾶς μηδαμῶς παρ᾿ ἀνθρώπων συντελείας πρὸς τὸ εἶναι δεομένων, τῶν δὲ ἀλόγων ἀρχομένων κατὰ φύσιν καὶ τὰς πρὸς ὃ πέφυκεν ἕκαστον χρείας ἀνθρώποις ἀποπληρούντων, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ αὖ τούτοις χρῆσθαι πεφυκότων· θέμις γὰρ οὔτε ἦν οὔτε ἐστὶ τὸ ἄρχον καὶ ἡγεμονοῦν ὑπάγειν εἰς χρῆσιν τοῖς ἐλάττοσιν, ἢ τὸ λογικὸν ὑποτάττειν ἀλόγοις, οὖσι πρὸς τὸ ἄρχειν ἀνεπιτηδείοις. Οὐκοῦν εἰ μήτε ἀναιτίως καὶ μάτην γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος (οὐδὲν γὰρ τῶν ὑπὸ θεοῦ γενομένων μάταιον, κατά γε τὴν τοῦ ποιήσαντος γνώμην), μήτε χρείας ἕνεκεν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν ὑπὸ θεοῦ γενομένων ποιημάτων, εὔδηλον ὅτι κατὰ μὲν τὸν πρῶτον καὶ κοινότερον λόγον δι᾿ ἑαυτὸν καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ πάσης τῆς δημιουργίας θεωρουμένην ἀγαθότητα καὶ σοφίαν ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, κατὰ δὲ τὸν προσεχέστερον τοῖς γενομένοις λόγον διὰ τὴν αὐτῶν τῶν γενομένων ζωήν, οὐκ ἐπὶ μικρὸν ἐξαπτομένην, εἶτα παντελῶς σβεννυμένην. Ἑρπετοῖς γάρ, οἶμαι, καὶ πτηνοῖς καὶ νηκτοῖς ἢ καὶ κοινότερον εἰπεῖν πᾶσι τοῖς ἀλόγοις τὴν τοιαύτην ζωὴν ἀπένειμεν ὁ θεός· τοῖς δὲ αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἀγαλματοφοροῦσι τὸν ποιητήν, νοῦν τε συνεπιφερομένοις καὶ λογικῆς κρίσεως μεμοιραμένοις, τὴν εἰς ἀεὶ διαμονὴν ἀπεκλήρωσεν ὁ ποιητής, ἵνα γινώσκοντες τὸν ἑαυτῶν ποιητὴν καὶ τὴν τούτου δύναμίν τε καὶ σοφίαν, νόμῳ τε συνεπόμενοι καὶ δίκῃ, τούτοις συνδιαιωνίζωσιν ἀπόνως οἷς τὴν προλαβοῦσαν ἐκράτυναν ζωήν, καίπερ ἐν φθαρτοῖς καὶ γηΐνοις ὄντες σώμασιν. Ὁπόσα μὲν γὰρ ἄλλου του χάριν γέγονεν, παυσαμένων ἐκείνων ὧν ἕνεκεν γέγονε, παύσεται εἰκότως καὶ αὐτὰ τὰ γενόμενα τοῦ εἶναι, καὶ οὐκ ἂν διαμένοι μάτην, ὡς ἂν μηδεμίαν ἐν τοῖς ὑπὸ θεοῦ γενομένοις τοῦ ματαίου χώραν ἔχοντος· τά γε μὴν δι᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ εἶναι καὶ ζῆν καθὼς πέφυκε γενόμενα, ὡς αὐτῆς τῆς αἰτίας τῇ φύσει συνειλημμένης καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτὸ μόνον τὸ εἶναι θεωρουμένης, οὐδεμίαν οὐδέποτε δέξαιτ᾿ ἂν τὴν τὸ εἶναι παντελῶς ἀφανίζουσαν αἰτίαν. Ταύτης δὲ ἐν τῷ εἶναι πάντοτε θεωρουμένης, δεῖ σώζεσθαι πάντως καὶ τὸ γενόμενον ζῶον, ἐνεργοῦν τε καὶ πάσχον ἃ πέφυκεν, ἑκατέρου τούτων ἐξ ὧν γέγονε τὰ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ συνεισφέροντος, καὶ τῆς μὲν ψυχῆς οὔσης τε καὶ διαμενούσης ὁμαλῶς ἐν ᾗ γέγονε φύσει, καὶ διαπονούσης ἃ πέφυκεν (πέφυκε δὲ ταῖς τοῦ σώματος ἐπιστατεῖν ὁρμαῖς καὶ τὸ προσπίπτον ἀεὶ τοῖς προσήκουσι κρίνειν καὶ μετρεῖν κριτηρίοις καὶ μέτροις), τοῦ δὲ σώματος κινουμένου κατὰ φύσιν πρὸς ἃ πέφυκεν, καὶ τὰς ἀποκληρωθείσας αὐτῷ δεχομένου μεταβολάς, μετὰ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν κατὰ τὰς ἡλικίας ἢ κατ᾿ εἶδος ἢ μέγεθος τὴν ἀνάστασιν. Εἶδος γάρ τι μεταβολῆς, καὶ πάντων ὕστατον, ἡ ἀνάστασις ἥ τε τῶν κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον περιόντων ἔτι πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον μεταβολή.
thought_title: Why God made the human being
orientation: Athenagoras is beginning the positive argument for resurrection from its cause, asking why God made the human being at all.
pass_a_gloss: The argument from the cause is this: if we examine whether the human being came to be simply and in vain or for the sake of something; and if for the sake of something, whether he came to be for this very thing, namely to live and to continue in the nature in which he came to be, or for the need of something; and if according to need, either the need of the maker himself or of some other of the things belonging to him and deemed worthy of greater care. Examining this more generally, we find that every person of sound mind, moved by rational judgment to do something, does nothing of the things he performs according to purpose in vain, but either for the sake of his own use or for the need of some other of the things he has cared for or for the sake of the thing itself that comes to be, being moved by some natural attraction and affection toward its generation; for example (let it be said through an image, so that the matter at hand may become clear) a human being makes a house for his own need, and he makes for oxen and camels or the other animals, of which he is in need, the shelter fitting for each of these, not for the sake of his own use according to what is apparent, but according to the end for this reason, and according to what is immediate for the care of these things he has cared for; and he begets children neither for his own need nor for the sake of some other of the things belonging to him, but so that those begotten by him may exist and continue as far as possible, consoling his own death by the succession of children and descendants and thinking by this to make the mortal immortal. But these things are done by these people. God, however, would not have made the human being in vain; for he is wise, and no work of wisdom is vain; nor for his own need; for he is without need of everything. And to the one who needs nothing at all, none of the things made by him would contribute to his own need. But neither did he make the human being for the sake of any of the works made by him. For none of the things that use reason and judgment, neither the greater nor the lesser, has come to be or comes to be for the need of another, but for the sake of the life and continuance of the very things that have come to be. For reason finds no need as the cause of the generation of human beings, since the immortal beings are without need and require no contribution at all from human beings for their existence, and the irrational beings are ruled according to nature and fulfill for human beings the needs for which each has been naturally fitted, but are not in turn naturally fitted to use these; for it was not and is not lawful to subject the ruling and governing thing to the use of the lesser things, or to subordinate the rational to the irrational, which are unfit for ruling. Therefore if the human being has come to be neither without cause and in vain (for nothing made by God is vain, at least according to the purpose of the maker), nor for the sake of the need of the maker himself or of some other of the works made by God, it is clear that according to the first and more general argument God made the human being for his own sake and for the goodness and wisdom observed in all creation, and according to the argument more immediate to the things that have come to be, for the life of the very things that have come to be, a life not kindled for a short time and then completely extinguished. For to creeping things, I think, and winged things and swimming things, or to speak more generally to all irrational beings, God assigned such a life; but to those who bear in themselves the image of the maker, and who carry along mind and have been allotted a share of rational judgment, the maker allotted continuance forever, so that knowing their own maker and his power and wisdom, and following law and justice, they may live forever with these things without distress, with which they strengthened their previous life, even though being in corruptible and earthly bodies. For as many things as have come to be for the sake of something else, when those things for whose sake they came to be have ceased, the things that came to be will reasonably also cease to exist, and would not continue in vain, since the vain has no place at all among the things made by God; but the things that have come to be for the very sake of existing and living as is natural, since the cause itself is bound up with the nature and is observed in the very fact of existing alone, would never admit any cause that completely destroys existence. And since this cause is always observed in existence, the living thing that has come to be must certainly be preserved, acting and being acted upon as is natural, each of these two things from which it came to be contributing what is its own, the soul both existing and continuing uniformly in the nature in which it came to be, and working at what is natural (and it is natural for it to preside over the impulses of the body and to judge and measure what always befalls it by fitting criteria and measures), and the body being moved according to nature toward what is natural, and receiving the changes allotted to it, and after the other changes according to ages or form or size, the resurrection. For the resurrection is a kind of change, and the last of all, and the change of those still surviving at that time to the better.

choices.why: Glossary term for the compound of soul and body; not used in this section but kept in mind for the argument.
Glossary term for lasting existence; renders the enduring existence of the whole human being.
Glossary term for the resurrection of dead human bodies.
Renders the compound literally as bearing the image of the maker within themselves, preserving the force of the verb.
Keeps the active force of the verb and the contrast between mortal and immortal.

choices.english: by some natural attraction and affection
choices.why: Renders both nouns literally, preserving the pair of motives.
rejected: by a natural pull and love

pass_b_english: The argument from cause runs like this. We must examine whether the human being came into existence simply and to no purpose, or for the sake of something. If for the sake of something, then we must ask whether that something is the very living and continuing in the nature in which he was made, or whether it is for the use of someone else. And if for use, then is it for the use of the maker himself, or of some other being that belongs to him and has been counted worthy of greater care?

When we consider this more broadly, we find that every person of sound mind who is moved by rational judgment to do something does nothing he undertakes on purpose to no end. He acts either for his own use, or for the need of some other being for whom he cares, or for the sake of the thing itself that comes into being, moved by some natural attraction and affection toward its existence. Let me use an illustration to make the point clear. A man builds a house for his own use. He also builds shelter suited to each of the animals he lacks, oxen, camels, and the rest. He does not build these for his own use, as it appears. In their final purpose they are for the animals' sake, but in their immediate purpose they are for the care of the animals he tends. He also begets children, not for his own use and not for the sake of anything else that belongs to him, but so that those born from him may exist and continue as long as possible. By the succession of children and descendants he consoles himself for his own death, and in this way he thinks he makes the mortal immortal.

But these examples come from human beings. God, however, would not have made the human being to no purpose, for he is wise, and no work of wisdom is pointless. Nor would he have made him for his own use, for he lacks nothing at all. To the one who needs nothing whatsoever, none of the things made by him could contribute anything for his own use. Nor did he make the human being for the sake of any of the works made by him. For none of the beings that use reason and judgment, whether greater or lesser, has come into being or comes into being for the use of another, but for the life and continuance of the beings themselves that have come to be.

Reason finds no need that could be the cause of the creation of human beings. The immortal beings lack nothing and have no need of any contribution from human beings for their existence. The irrational animals are by nature ruled, and they fulfill for human beings the uses for which each was made by nature, but they are not by nature meant to make use of human beings in turn. For it was not and is not lawful for what rules and leads to be subjected to the use of what is lesser, or for the rational to be subordinated to the irrational, which are unfit to rule.

Therefore, if the human being did not come into being without cause and to no purpose, for nothing made by God is pointless, at least according to the purpose of the maker, and if he did not come into being for the use of the maker himself or of any other of the works made by God, then it is clear that, according to the first and more general account, God made the human being for his own sake and for the goodness and wisdom seen throughout all creation. According to the account more immediate to the things made, he made him for the life of the beings themselves that came into being, a life not kindled for a short time and then completely extinguished.

For to creeping things, I think, and to winged creatures and swimming creatures, or to speak more generally, to all irrational beings, God assigned such a life. But to those who bear in themselves the image of their maker, who carry with them a mind and share in rational judgment, the maker allotted an everlasting continuance. He did this so that, knowing their maker and his power and wisdom, and following law and justice, they might continue forever without distress together with those things by which they confirmed their previous life, even while they were in corruptible and earthly bodies.

For whatever has come into being for the sake of something else will reasonably cease to exist when those things for whose sake it came into being cease, and it would not continue to no purpose, since nothing pointless has any place among the things made by God. But things that came into being for the very sake of existing and living as their nature requires, since their cause is bound up with their nature and is seen in their very existence, could never admit any cause that completely destroys their existence.

Since this cause is always seen in their existence, the living being that has come into being must certainly be preserved, acting and being acted upon as its nature requires. Each of the two parts from which it was made contributes what belongs to it. The soul exists and continues unchanged in the nature in which it was made, and it works at what it is fitted for. For it is its nature to preside over the impulses of the body and to judge and measure whatever befalls it by the proper criteria and measures. The body moves according to nature toward what it is fitted for, and receives the changes allotted to it. Along with the other changes according to the stages of life or form or size, it receives the resurrection. For the resurrection is a kind of change, and the last of all, and the change of those still living at that time to the better.

problems.quote: they might live forever without toil in the things by which they strengthened their previous life
problems.source_quote: τούτοις συνδιαιωνίζωσιν ἀπόνως οἷς τὴν προλαβοῦσαν ἐκράτυναν ζωήν
problems.why: 'In the things by which they strengthened' misreads οἷς (dative of means/instrument) as 'in which'; 'live forever without toil by the same means by which they strengthened' or 'through which'.
problems.fix: live forever without toil by those same means through which they strengthened their previous life
problems.ruling: οἷς is dative of means/instrument ('by which'), not 'in which'; 'in the things by which' conflates locative and instrumental, slightly misleading.

problems.quote: and for those still living at that time it is a change to the better
problems.source_quote: ἥ τε τῶν κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον περιόντων ἔτι πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον μεταβολή
problems.why: English omits ἥτε...μεταβολή as parallel to resurrection; 'and [there is] the change of those still surviving at that time to the better'. The 'it is' makes this a predicate about resurrection rather than a second kind of change.
problems.fix: and there is also the change of those still living at that time to the better
problems.ruling: ἥ τε...μεταβολή is a second nominative parallel to ἡ ἀνάστασις, not a predicate; 'it is a change' misreads the grammar, losing the structural parallel.

problems.quote: and receives the changes allotted to it, and along with the other changes that come with age or form or size, it receives the resurrection
problems.source_quote: καὶ τὰς ἀποκληρωθείσας αὐτῷ δεχομένου μεταβολάς, μετὰ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν κατὰ τὰς ἡλικίας ἢ κατ᾿ εἶδος ἢ μέγεθος τὴν ἀνάστασιν
problems.why: English misses μετὰ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων...τὴν ἀνάστασιν structure: 'after the others [changes] according to ages or form or size, [it receives] the resurrection'. 'Along with' makes resurrection concurrent rather than subsequent.
problems.fix: and receives the changes allotted to it; and after the others that come with age or form or size, it receives the resurrection
problems.ruling: μετὰ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων...τὴν ἀνάστασιν means 'after the other changes...the resurrection'; 'along with' wrongly makes resurrection concurrent, not subsequent.

edits.old: they might live forever without toil in the things by which they strengthened their previous life
edits.new: they might live forever without toil by those same means through which they strengthened their previous life

edits.old: and for those still living at that time it is a change to the better
edits.new: and there is also the change of those still living at that time to the better

edits.old: and receives the changes allotted to it, and along with the other changes that come with age or form or size, it receives the resurrection
edits.new: and receives the changes allotted to it; and after the others that come with age or form or size, it receives the resurrection

problems.why: συνδιαιωνίζωσιν means 'continue forever with', not 'live forever'; ἀπόνως means 'without toil/painlessly'.
problems.fix: continue forever without toil together with those things

problems.quote: by those same means through which they strengthened their previous life
problems.why: οἷς is dative of instrument/association, 'with which'; ἐκράτυναν means 'confirmed/established', not 'strengthened'.
problems.fix: with which they confirmed their previous life

problems.quote: after the others that come with age or form or size, it receives the resurrection
problems.source_quote: μετὰ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν κατὰ τὰς ἡλικίας ἢ κατ᾿ εἶδος ἢ μέγεθος τὴν ἀνάστασιν
problems.why: μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων means 'along with the others', not 'after the others'; κατὰ τὰς ἡλικίας means 'according to the stages of life/ages'.
problems.fix: and along with the other changes according to the stages of life or form or size, the resurrection

problems.quote: and there is also the change of those still living at that time to the better
problems.source_quote: ἥ τε τῶν κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον περιόντων ἔτι πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον μεταβολή
problems.why: This clause is incomplete in Greek; ἥ τε connects it as 'both...and', but English omits the correlative structure and makes it a separate sentence, losing the grammar.
problems.fix: and both the change of those still living at that time to the better

problems.quote: For the resurrection is a kind of change, and the last of all changes
problems.source_quote: Εἶδος γάρ τι μεταβολῆς, καὶ πάντων ὕστατον, ἡ ἀνάστασις
problems.why: The English omits 'γάρ' force ('for') and makes two separate clauses, but more importantly misses that ἡ ἀνάστασις is the subject delayed for emphasis: 'for a kind of change, and the last of all, is the resurrection'.
problems.fix: For a kind of change, and the last of all, is the resurrection

edits.old: they might live forever without toil by those same means through which they strengthened their previous life
edits.new: they might continue forever without toil together with those things by which they confirmed their previous life

edits.old: and after the others that come with age or form or size, it receives the resurrection
edits.new: and along with the other changes according to the stages of life or form or size, the resurrection

edits.old: For the resurrection is a kind of change, and the last of all changes, and there is also the change of those still living at that time to the better.
edits.new: For a kind of change, and the last of all, is the resurrection, and both the change of those still living at that time to the better.

fixed: The first problem was real: the English 'live forever' missed the force of συνδιαιωνίζωσιν ('continue forever with'), and 'strengthened' missed the force of ἐκράτυναν ('confirmed').

The second problem was real: 'after the others' missed the force of μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων ('along with the others'), and 'come with age' missed the force of κατὰ τὰς ἡλικίας ('according to the stages of life').
The third problem was real: the English lost the delayed subject structure of the Greek and the correlative force of ἥ τε, so the final clause was made into a separate sentence.

problems.why: 'Without toil' is possible but ἀπόνως here likely means 'without pain/distress' given resurrection context; 'toil' is too narrow.

problems.quote: both the change of those still living at that time to the better
problems.source_quote: ἥ τε τῶν κατ' ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον περιόντων ἔτι πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον μεταβολή
problems.why: Incomplete sentence; 'both...' lacks a second term, and 'change' singular obscures that two changes are mentioned (resurrection and transformation).
problems.fix: both the resurrection and the transformation of those still living at that time to the better
problems.ruling: τε ('both') pairs ἀνάστασις with μεταβολή; English 'both' lacks second term, leaving sentence incomplete and misleading.

edits.old: they might continue forever without toil together with those things by which they confirmed their previous life
edits.new: they might continue forever without distress together with those things by which they confirmed their previous life

edits.old: For a kind of change, and the last of all, is the resurrection, and both the change of those still living at that time to the better.
edits.new: For the resurrection is a kind of change, and the last of all, and the change of those still living at that time to the better.

fixed: The 'both' issue was resolved by removing 'both' and restoring the sentence structure to match the source, which lists resurrection and the change of the living as a single final clause.
The 'without toil' issue was resolved by changing 'toil' to 'distress' in both the English and the gloss.

problems.quote: but in its final purpose for that reason, and in its immediate purpose for the care of the animals he tends
problems.why: Syntax is tangled; meaning is unclear.
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'ultimately for the animals' sake, though immediately for their care.'

edits.old: but in its final purpose for that reason, and in its immediate purpose for the care of the animals he tends
edits.new: but ultimately for the animals' sake, though immediately for their care

fixed: The English was unclear; the source (κατὰ μὲν τὸ τέλος διὰ τοῦτο, κατὰ δὲ τὸ προσεχὲς διὰ τὴν τούτων ὧν πεφρόντικεν ἐπιμέλειαν) means the final purpose is for the animals themselves, while the immediate purpose is their care. Rewrote for clarity.

refereed.quote: He also builds shelter suited to each of the animals he lacks—oxen, camels, and the rest
refereed.source_quote: ποιεῖ δὲ βουσὶ καὶ καμήλοις ἢ τοῖς ἄλλοις ζώοις, ὧν ἐστιν ἐνδεής, τὴν ἑκάστῳ τούτων ἁρμόζουσαν σκέπην
refereed.why: He builds shelters for the oxen, camels, and other animals he needs, not 'animals he lacks.' ἐνδεής means 'in need of,' not 'lacking' here.
refereed.fix: He also builds for oxen, camels, and the other animals he needs a shelter suited to each of them
refereed.ruling: ἐνδεής + genitive ὧν means 'in need of,' not 'lacking'; 'animals he lacks' reverses meaning.

polish.changed: Clarified the tangled sentence about building shelters for animals by separating final and immediate purposes, made pronoun references explicit, and smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim.
